danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Der var gået fire uger, siden Pierre var blevet taget til fange, og selvom franskmændene havde tilbudt at flytte ham fra de meniges skur til officerernes, var han blevet i det skur, han først var blevet anbragt i.

I det nedbrændte og ødelagte Moskva oplevede Pierre næsten de yderste grænser for de afsavn, et menneske kan udholde. Men takket være sin fysiske styrke og sit helbred, som han indtil da ikke havde været bevidst om, og især fordi afsavnene kom så gradvist, at det var umuligt at sige, hvornår de begyndte, bar han sin situation ikke blot let, men ligefrem med glæde. Og netop nu opnåede han den sindsro og indre fred, som han tidligere forgæves havde stræbt efter. Han havde længe søgt den sjælefred og indre harmoni, der havde gjort så dybt indtryk på ham hos soldaterne ved Borodino. Han havde søgt den i filantropi, i frimureri, i hovedstadens adspredelser, i vin, i heroiske selvopofringer og i romantisk kærlighed til Natasja — han havde søgt den gennem fornuft — og alle disse forsøg var slået fejl. Og nu havde han uden at tænke over det fundet den fred og indre harmoni udelukkende gennem dødens rædsel, gennem afsavn og gennem det, han genkendte i Karatajev.

De forfærdelige øjeblikke, han havde gennemlevet under henrettelserne, havde så at sige for altid vasket de urolige tanker og følelser ud af hans fantasi og hukommelse, tanker der tidligere havde forekommet så vigtige. Det faldt ham ikke længere ind at tænke på Rusland, krigen, politik eller Napoleon. Det stod ham klart, at alle disse ting ikke vedkom ham, og at han hverken var kaldet til at dømme om dem eller kunne gøre det. »Rusland og sommervejr hører ikke sammen,« tænkte han og gentog Karatajevs ord, som han fandt mærkeligt trøstende. Hans forsæt om at dræbe Napoleon og hans beregninger af Apokalypsens dyrs kabalistiske tal forekom ham nu meningsløse og ligefrem latterlige. Hans vrede mod sin kone og hans angst for, at hans navn skulle blive plettet, virkede nu ikke blot ubetydeligt, men nærmest morsomt. Hvad kom det ham ved, at den kvinde et eller andet sted levede det liv, hun foretrak? Hvad betød det for nogen, og især for ham, om de fandt ud af, at deres fanges navn var grev Bezukhov?

Han tænkte nu ofte på sin samtale med fyrst Andrej og var helt enig med ham, selvom han forstod fyrst Andrejs tanker lidt anderledes. Fyrst Andrej havde tænkt og sagt, at lykke kun kunne være negativ, men han havde sagt det med et skær af bitterhed og ironi, som om han i virkeligheden mente, at al stræben efter positiv lykke blot er indplantet i os for at pine os og aldrig kan tilfredsstilles. Men Pierre troede det uden forbehold. Fraværet af lidelse, tilfredsstillelsen af ens behov og den deraf følgende frihed i valget af beskæftigelse — det vil sige ens livsform — syntes Pierre nu utvivlsomt at udgøre menneskets højeste lykke. Her og nu satte han for første gang fuld pris på glæden ved at spise, når han ville spise, drikke, når han ville drikke, sove, når han ville sove, varme, når han frøs, og tale med et medmenneske, når han ønskede at tale og høre en menneskelig stemme. Tilfredsstillelsen af ens behov — god mad, renlighed og frihed — nu da han var berøvet alt dette, syntes Pierre at udgøre fuldkommen lykke. Og valget af beskæftigelse — det vil sige ens livsform — nu da det var så begrænset, forekom ham så let, at han glemte, at en overflod af livets bekvemmeligheder ødelægger al glæde ved at tilfredsstille sine behov, ligesom stor frihed i valget af beskæftigelse — den frihed som hans rigdom, uddannelse og sociale position havde givet ham — netop gør valget uløseligt vanskeligt og ødelægger ønsket om og muligheden for at have en beskæftigelse.

Alle Pierres dagdrømme drejede sig nu om den tid, han ville være fri. Men senere, og resten af sit liv, tænkte og talte han med begejstring om den måned i fangenskab, om de uigenkaldelige, stærke, glade fornemmelser og først og fremmest om den fuldstændige sindsro og indre frihed, som han kun oplevede i de uger.

Da han den første dag stod tidligt op og gik ud af skuret i daggry og så Jomfruklostrerets kupler og kors, der endnu var mørke, rimfrosten på det støvede græs, Spurvebakkerne og de skovklædte skrænter over den bugtende flod, der forsvandt i den lilla horisont — da han mærkede den friske luft og hørte kragernes skrig, mens de fløj fra Moskva hen over marken, og da lyset siden brød frem fra øst, og solens rand dukkede højtideligt op bag en sky, og kuplerne og korsene, rimfrosten, horisonten og floden alt sammen begyndte at funkle i det glade lys — da følte Pierre en ny glæde og livskraft, som han aldrig før havde kendt. Og den forblev ikke blot hos ham under hele fangenskabet, men voksede sig endda stærkere, efterhånden som hans lidelser tiltog.

Den følelse af årvågenhed og parathed til alt blev yderligere styrket af den høje mening, hans medfanger fik om ham kort efter hans ankomst til skuret. Med sit sprogkendskab, den respekt franskmændene viste ham, hans beskedenhed, hans villighed til at give alt, hvad der blev bedt om (han modtog den ugentlige ration på tre rubler, der blev givet til officerer), sin styrke — som han demonstrerede for soldaterne ved at trykke søm ind i skurets vægge — sin venlighed mod kammeraterne og sin evne til at sidde stille og tænke uden at foretage sig noget (hvilket forekom dem ubegribeligt), fremstod han for dem som et noget mystisk og overlegent væsen. Netop de egenskaber, der havde været til hindring, ja ligefrem skadelige for ham i den verden, han havde levet i — hans styrke, hans foragt for livets bekvemmeligheder, hans åndsfraværelse og ligefremhed — gav ham her blandt disse mennesker næsten status som en helt. Og Pierre mærkede, at deres mening lagde ansvar på ham.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Four weeks had passed since Pierre had been taken prisoner. Though the French had offered to transfer him from the soldiers' shed to the officers' quarters, he had stayed in the shed where he'd first been placed.

In burned and devastated Moscow, Pierre experienced nearly the furthest limits of deprivation a person can endure. But thanks to his physical strength and health—which he'd been unaware of until now—and especially because the hardships came so gradually that it was impossible to say when they began, he bore his situation not only easily but even joyfully. And it was precisely now that he found the peace of mind and inner harmony he had previously strived for in vain. He had long sought it in different ways—in philanthropy, in Freemasonry, in the distractions of city life, in wine, in heroic self-sacrifice, and in his romantic love for Natasha. He had sought it through reason—and all these attempts had failed him. Now, without thinking about it, he had found that peace and inner harmony only through the horror of death, through deprivation, and through what he recognized in Karataev.

Those terrible moments he had lived through at the executions had washed away from his mind, as if forever, the anxious thoughts and feelings that had once seemed so important. It no longer occurred to him to think about Russia, or the war, or politics, or Napoleon. It was obvious to him that none of these were his concern, that he had no business judging them, and therefore couldn't. 'Russia and summer weather don't come tied together,' he thought, repeating Karataev's words, which he found strangely comforting. His intention of killing Napoleon and his calculations about the number of the Beast in Revelation now seemed meaningless and even ridiculous. His anger at his wife, his worry about his name being dishonored—these seemed not just trivial but amusing. What did it matter to him that some woman somewhere was living as she pleased? What did it matter to anyone, especially him, whether they discovered that their prisoner's name was Count Bezukhov?

He now often recalled his conversation with Prince Andrew and completely agreed with him, though he understood Andrew's thoughts somewhat differently. Prince Andrew had said that happiness could only be negative, but he'd said it with a shade of bitterness and irony, as though he were really saying that the desire for positive happiness is planted in us only to torment us and never be satisfied. But Pierre believed this without any mental reservation. The absence of suffering, the satisfaction of one's needs, and the consequent freedom to choose one's occupation—that is, one's way of life—now seemed to Pierre to be unquestionably the highest human happiness. Here and now, for the first time, he fully appreciated the pleasure of eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, sleeping when tired, warmth when cold, and talking to another person when he wanted to hear a human voice. The satisfaction of one's needs—good food, cleanliness, freedom—now that he was deprived of all this, seemed to Pierre to constitute perfect happiness. And the choice of occupation—now that this was so restricted—seemed such a simple matter that he forgot how an excess of life's comforts destroys the joy of meeting one's needs, and how great freedom in choosing one's path—the kind his wealth, education, and social position had given him—is exactly what makes that choice impossibly difficult and kills the desire and ability to have any occupation at all.

All Pierre's daydreams now centered on the time when he would be free. Yet for the rest of his life, he thought and spoke with deep feeling about that month of captivity—those irretrievable, powerful, joyful sensations, and above all the complete peace of mind and inner freedom he experienced only during those weeks.

When on the first day he rose early, stepped out of the shed at dawn, and saw the domes and crosses of the New Convent of the Virgin still dark against the sky, the hoarfrost on the dusty grass, the Sparrow Hills, and the wooded banks above the winding river fading into the purple distance; when he felt the touch of fresh air and heard the crows flying from Moscow across the field; and when light flared from the east and the sun's rim appeared solemnly from behind a cloud, and the domes and crosses, the frost, the distance, and the river all began to sparkle in the joyful light—Pierre felt a new strength and joy in life such as he had never known. And this feeling not only stayed with him throughout his imprisonment but even grew stronger as his hardships increased.

That alertness and readiness for anything was further strengthened by the high opinion his fellow prisoners formed of him soon after his arrival. His knowledge of languages, the respect the French showed him, his simplicity, his willingness to give away anything asked of him (he received the officers' allowance of three rubles a week), his strength (which he demonstrated by pressing nails into the hut's walls), his gentleness toward his companions, and his ability to sit still and think without doing anything (which struck them as mysterious)—all this gave him an almost heroic status among them. The very qualities that had been a hindrance, even harmful, in his former world—his strength, his indifference to comfort, his absent-mindedness and simplicity—here, among these people, made him nearly a hero. And Pierre felt that their opinion placed responsibilities on him.
